title: One Protein From Receptor to Gene

scenes.tts: Add interferon to human cells, and a set of genes switches on within minutes. Interferon is a protein that warns cells of a virus. The genes still switch on when a drug stops the cells from making any new protein. So every part of the path, from the cell surface to those genes, must already be in the cell, waiting. What is the path made of?
scenes.visual: A cell: membrane on top, nucleus and DNA below. Interferon lands, the genes turn green and a clock sweeps. Reset: interferon lifts off, a drug strikes out new protein, interferon returns and the genes turn on again. A dashed path of unknown parts fills in from surface to DNA.
scenes.narration: Add interferon to human cells, and a set of genes switches on within minutes. Interferon is a protein that warns cells of a virus. The genes still switch on when a drug stops the cells from making any new protein. So every part of the path, from the cell surface to those genes, must already be in the cell, waiting. What is the path made of?

scenes.tts: Interferon is a cytokine. A cytokine is a small secreted protein that tells other cells what to do. Each chain of a cytokine receptor crosses the membrane once, and it has no enzyme at all. Instead, its inside tail holds a separate tyrosine kinase. This kinase is called a Jak, and it is there before any cytokine arrives.
scenes.visual: The interferon chip becomes a cytokine chip and steps aside. One receptor chain grows through the membrane, an empty dashed slot shows it has no enzyme, then a JAK blob appears on its tail; a second chain with its JAK joins it.
scenes.narration: Interferon is a cytokine. A cytokine is a small secreted protein that tells other cells what to do. Each chain of a cytokine receptor crosses the membrane once, and it has no enzyme at all. Instead, its inside tail holds a separate tyrosine kinase. This kinase is called a JAK, and it is there before any cytokine arrives.
scenes.caption: Interferon is a cytokine. A cytokine is a small secreted protein that tells other cells what to do. Each chain of a cytokine receptor crosses the membrane once, and it has no enzyme at all. Instead, its inside tail holds a separate tyrosine kinase. This kinase is called a JAK, and it is there before any cytokine arrives.

scenes.tts: Binding does one job. The cytokine sets two receptor chains, and so two Jaks, in position against each other. Now the two Jaks are close enough to phosphorylate each other. Each adds a phosphate to its partner, and both become fully active. A receptor with no enzyme of its own has borrowed one.
scenes.visual: The cytokine lands and the two chains slide into position, bringing the JAKs together. A phosphate crosses each way between the JAKs and both outlines turn green.

scenes.tts: The active Jaks now phosphorylate tyrosines along the receptor tails. These phosphorylated tyrosines are docking sites. A protein called a Stat waits in the cytoplasm. It carries an S H 2 domain, a module that binds a phosphate on a tyrosine. With that domain, the Stat docks on the receptor tail, next to the Jak.
scenes.visual: A phosphate slides from each JAK down to the end of its receptor tail. Two STAT blobs wait in the cytoplasm; the pink SH2 cup on each is named, then each STAT rises and its cup closes on a tail phosphate.
scenes.narration: The active JAKs now phosphorylate tyrosines along the receptor tails. These phosphorylated tyrosines are docking sites. A protein called a STAT waits in the cytoplasm. It carries an SH2 domain, a module that binds a phosphate on a tyrosine. With that domain, the STAT docks on the receptor tail, next to the JAK.
scenes.caption: The active JAKs now phosphorylate tyrosines along the receptor tails. These phosphorylated tyrosines are docking sites. A protein called a STAT waits in the cytoplasm. It carries an SH2 domain, a module that binds a phosphate on a tyrosine. With that domain, the STAT docks on the receptor tail, next to the JAK.

scenes.tts: The Jak then adds one phosphate to the docked Stat, on a single tyrosine. Now the same S H 2 domain has something new to hold. It holds the phosphorylated tyrosine of a partner Stat instead, and the partner does the same in return. Two grips hold the pair, where one grip held the Stat to the receptor. So the same domain is used twice.
scenes.visual: A phosphate drops from each JAK onto each docked STAT. The STATs let go, turn to face each other and lock: each pink cup holds the other's phosphate. One grip at the receptor is compared with two grips in the pair.

So the same domain is used twice.

scenes.tts: The pair enters the nucleus, binds a specific DNA sequence, and switches on transcription. Now count the proteins between the receptor complex and the gene. There is one, with no second messenger and no chain of kinases. That is why genes can answer within minutes. So keep this rule: one protein, with one phosphate, carries the signal from receptor to gene.
scenes.visual: The STAT pair crosses into the nucleus, settles on the DNA and the gene turns green. A column counts receptor complex, one STAT, gene; a ghost second messenger and a ghost kinase chain are crossed out; the clock returns; a single arrow runs from receptor to DNA.
